findings.quote: **Trade-off.** All AWS access depends on the identity provider. Callvale keeps one tested emergency path [through direct federation](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-emergency-access-direct-federation).
findings.evidence: The sentence presents direct federation as the answer to a dependency on the identity provider, but direct federation uses the same identity provider. The linked fact's own scope is 'IAM Identity Center unavailable, IAM data plane and external IdP available'. Source docs/singlesignon/latest/userguide/emergency-access: "This configuration works when IAM Identity Center is unavailable, but the IAM data plane and your external identity provider (IdP) are available . If you prefer to not depend on the external IdP, consider setting up AWS break-glass access". RULINGS: 'The story never teaches a fact ... if the canon disagrees, keep the decision and change the stated reason.' Fix: 'All AWS access depends on IAM Identity Center and the identity provider. Callvale keeps one tested emergency path through direct federation for an IAM Identity Center disruption' (and, if wanted, a break-glass path for an identity provider outage, which needs a new fact from the emergency-access page). The same reason recurs in 2-deep.md 'Why keep direct federation?' (that sentence is correct: it names IAM Identity Center, not the IdP).
findings.resolution: Trade-off now reads 'AWS access depends on IAM Identity Center and the identity provider. For an IAM Identity Center outage, Callvale keeps a tested emergency path [through direct federation].' The decision is kept (STARTUP.md); the stated reason now matches the fact's scope. A break-glass path for an IdP outage was not added: 2-deep.md is at its cap (2,396 of 2,400 words).

findings.quote: **Twin.** If the stem said "Amazon RDS for SQL Server databases must use Windows Authentication with the employees' existing AD accounts" instead: AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a trust, because RDS is [compatible with AWS Managed Microsoft AD only](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-rds-needs-managed-ad).
findings.evidence: The 'only' comes from the Directory Service page 'Application compatibility policy for AD Connector' and is true only among the Directory Service options (Managed AD versus AD Connector). The RDS User Guide documents joining RDS for SQL Server directly to a self-managed AD: source full:amazonrds-userguide (section 'Joining your DB instance to self-managed Active Directory'): "To join your RDS for SQL Server DB instance to your self-managed AD, follow these steps:" and (section 'Requirements'): "Make sure you've met the following requirements before joining an RDS for SQL Server DB instance to your self-managed AD domain." The Directory Service page itself links 'Join Amazon RDS for SQL Server to your self-managed Active Directory' (docs/directoryservice/latest/admin-guide/usecase1). So the twin's reason is false as written, and with 'existing AD accounts' a direct join to the on-premises domain is a second valid answer. Same bare claim in data/05-identity-federation/speak.json identity-federation-s02 kp4 ('Amazon RDS is compatible with AWS Managed Microsoft AD only') and its must_not_say 'correct' text. Fix: either qualify ('of the Directory Service options, RDS works with AWS Managed Microsoft AD, not AD Connector', linking directory-service-ad-connector-not-rds-sql-server) or rewrite the twin so that the stem excludes a self-managed join (for example, 'the on-premises domain controllers will be retired'); request a fact for the RDS self-managed AD join.
findings.resolution: q003 twin (wording only; stem, options and key unchanged, so no new verification) now reads 'If the stem said "Amazon RDS for SQL Server databases must use Windows Authentication through a directory that AWS manages" instead: AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a trust, because AD Connector is [not compatible with RDS SQL Server]'; q003 facts swap directory-service-rds-needs-managed-ad for directory-service-ad-connector-not-rds-sql-server. speak s02 (ten_second, sixty_second, skeleton, kp4, must_not_say) no longer says 'only'. The 'only' link is gone from the prose and every shipped item. RDS joining a self-managed AD directly is not stated: no verified fact holds it, and a fact request would stay open at finalize (B09). For the registrar: a fact from docs/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_SQLServer_SelfManagedActiveDirectory, and a scope note on directory-service-rds-needs-managed-ad (still linked only by the rejected q008).

findings.quote: > **Exam signal:** "RDS for SQL Server with Windows Authentication" points to AWS Managed Microsoft AD, to [Run Active Directory dependent workloads in AWS](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-decision-guide-ad-dependent-workloads-row).
findings.evidence: Same evidence as claims-002 (full:amazonrds-userguide: "To join your RDS for SQL Server DB instance to your self-managed AD, follow these steps:"). The signal, the table row 'Amazon RDS for SQL Server | Yes: [compatible with AWS Managed Microsoft AD only] | No' (same subsection) and the 1-fast.md Signals row 'users must stay in the on-premises Active Directory' with 'But not if: RDS for SQL Server: AWS Managed Microsoft AD' state the Directory Service comparison as if it were the only RDS option. Within a Managed-AD-versus-AD-Connector table it is fine; add 'of the Directory Service options' or 'not AD Connector' to the signal and the But-not-if cell.
findings.resolution: 2-deep table: RDS row is 'Yes, with [either a one-way or two-way trust]' | 'No: [not compatible with RDS SQL Server]'. Exam signal: '"RDS for SQL Server with Windows Authentication" points to AWS Managed Microsoft AD, not AD Connector: it is [not compatible with RDS SQL Server].' The 1-fast But-not-if cell of that row now names the case that flips it: 'several forests: AWS Managed Microsoft AD, to [support multiple domains or forests]'.

findings.quote: 4. **Call AWS.** A **bucket** **policy** with the user's identity ID gives each user [access to their own folder](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-identity-id-per-user-s3-folder).
findings.evidence: The documented pattern is an identity-based policy on the identity pool's role with the ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} variable, and the chapter's own answer to identity-federation-q002 says 'give the authenticated role access to the prefix that matches each identity ID'. Source full:iam-userguide (section 'Amazon S3: Allows Amazon Cognito users to access objects in their bucket'): "This example shows how you might create an identity-based policy that allows Amazon Cognito users to access objects in a specific Amazon S3 bucket." and "The 'sub' value used in the object key is not the user's sub value in the User Pool, it is the identity id associated with the user in the Identity Pool." The linked FAQ sentence ('a policy for an S3 bucket') is ambiguous and does not say bucket policy. A reader who learns 'bucket policy' here meets the opposite in Question 3. Fix: 'A policy on the authenticated role, with the user's identity ID in the path, gives each user access to their own folder.'
findings.resolution: Step 4 now reads 'A policy with the user's identity ID in the folder path gives each user [access to their own folder].' ('bucket policy' removed; Question 3 teaches the role policy). For the registrar: the claim of cognito-identity-id-per-user-s3-folder says 'S3 bucket policy', while its FAQ quote says only 'a policy for an S3 bucket'.

findings.quote: Not yet. Identities [must be provisioned into IAM Identity Center](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-provision-before-assign) first. Turn on SCIM.
findings.evidence: The question asks 'Can she get a permission set today?' and the answer implies SCIM is the only way to provision. Manual provisioning exists: source docs/singlesignon/latest/userguide/provision-automatically: "In those cases, you can manually provision users through the IAM Identity Center console. When you add users to IAM Identity Center, ensure that you set the user name to be identical to the user name that you have in your IdP." The chapter's own identity-federation-q004 twin ('new hires are added by hand') assumes manual provisioning. Fix: 'Only after an administrator provisions her: create her user by hand with the same user name, or turn on SCIM so that new users appear automatically.'
findings.resolution: The Stop and answer now asks 'What must happen before she gets a permission set?'; answer: 'Provisioning: identities [must be provisioned into IAM Identity Center] first. SCIM does it for you.' SCIM is no longer a precondition. Manual provisioning is not stated, because no verified fact holds it.

findings.quote: **Check 2.** Does AWS keep a copy of the users that AD Connector serves?
findings.evidence: The answer 'No. AWS does not replicate any of your directory data' is true of Directory Service, but this chapter's main use of AD Connector is as the IAM Identity Center identity source, and IAM Identity Center then synchronizes users and groups (not passwords) into its own store. Fact iam-identity-center-configurable-ad-sync-scope: "IAM Identity Center configurable Active Directory (AD) sync enables you to explicitly configure the identities in Microsoft Active Directory that are automatically synchronized into IAM Identity Center and control the synchronization process." Fact iam-identity-center-ad-pass-through-no-passwords-synced (claim: 'it synchronizes users, groups and memberships, but no password information'). Same problem in data/05-identity-federation/speak.json identity-federation-s02 kp2 accept 'no copy of the users in AWS' and the 60-second line 'It keeps no copy of your users in AWS'. Fix: ask 'Does Directory Service keep a copy ...' or add 'IAM Identity Center, when connected, copies users and groups, never passwords.'
findings.resolution: 1-fast Check 2 now asks what an app with user pool tokens needs to write to Amazon S3. speak s02: the line is now 'Your directory data stays on those domain controllers.' and kp2 accepts 'the directory data stays in your office'.

findings.quote: **The problem it solves.** Without them, each AWS account needs IAM users, and each app stores passwords.
findings.evidence: Unlinked claim that contradicts the chapter's own subsection 'Direct SAML federation works per account while Identity Center federates once'. Fact iam-identity-center-decision-guide-federation-with-iam: "You can also use IAM to federate workforce users through your identity provider to specific AWS accounts. Users assume IAM roles to perform scoped actions on the AWS resources in the account." Fact iam-federation-saml-console-sso-without-iam-users (linked in 2-deep.md as 'without an IAM user for everyone in the organization'). Fix: 'Without them, you manage access account by account, and each app stores passwords.'
findings.resolution: 1-fast 'The problem it solves' now reads 'Without them, you manage access account by account, and each app stores passwords.'

findings.quote: If a database or file share in AWS must join the domain, choose Managed AD.
findings.evidence: The model answer's rule is broader than the facts it cites. FSx for Windows File Server can join a self-managed AD: fact directory-service-fsx-windows-needs-managed-ad-or-self-managed quotes "Amazon FSx provides two options using your FSx for Windows File Server file system with Active Directory: Using Amazon FSx with AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory and Using a self-managed Microsoft Active Directory." RDS for SQL Server can too (claims-002). And EC2 instances can join through AD Connector: fact directory-service-which-to-choose-row quotes "You can also use AD Connector to join Amazon EC2 instances to your existing Active Directory domain." The ten_second answer ('For workloads like RDS for SQL Server, use AWS Managed Microsoft AD') has the same gap. Fix: 'If RDS for SQL Server or FSx must use a directory that AWS runs, choose Managed AD; AD Connector does not work with them.'
findings.resolution: speak s02 (speak add --replace): sixty_second 'For RDS for SQL Server, choose Managed AD. FSx for Windows can also join your own domain.'; ten_second 'For RDS for SQL Server, use AWS Managed Microsoft AD: AD Connector does not serve it.'; kp4 now names FSx with Managed AD or your own AD (fact directory-service-fsx-windows-needs-managed-ad-or-self-managed).

findings.quote: - "Put an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API in ...": It works, but the team writes and runs SAML code that the user pool and the load balancer provide without code.
findings.evidence: No fact supports 'It works'. The stem keeps an internet-facing Application Load Balancer, so requests can still reach the load balancer and the instances without passing the HTTP API, which breaks 'before any request reaches the instances'; and no fact says a Lambda authorizer receives SAML assertions (a SAML assertion goes to the service provider's ACS URL, fact cognito-saml-idp-must-support-saml-2). Rule: a 'why not' that grants an option 'works' must be true (TOOLS-rules item rationale). Fix: 'The load balancer stays internet-facing, so requests can bypass the API, and the team writes SAML code that the user pool and the load balancer provide without code.'
findings.resolution: q010 option d why (wording only) now reads 'It adds code to write and run: the team builds SAML handling that the user pool and the load balancer provide without code. The load balancer also stays internet-facing beside the API.' 'It works' is gone. The option text is unchanged: changing it needs a new verification round.

findings.quote: Amazon Cognito is [not a supported identity source](../facts/iam-identity-center.md#iam-identity-center-cognito-is-not-an-identity-source) of IAM Identity Center, and it serves customer-facing applications, not the workforce.
findings.evidence: 'not the workforce' contradicts fact cognito-user-pool-workforce-sso-in-your-app: "You can provide single sign-on (SSO) in your app for your organization's workforce identities in SAML 2.0 and OIDC IdPs with user pools." The chapter itself teaches this in 2-deep.md ('partner employees sign in ... points to a user pool, for workforce identities in SAML 2.0 and OIDC IdPs'). Fix: 'it signs users in to your apps, not workforce users in to AWS accounts.'
findings.resolution: q001 option b why now reads 'Cognito is built for [customer identity and access management (CIAM)] in the apps you build. The engineers need one sign-in to every account and the AWS CLI, which IAM Identity Center gives.' Fact cognito-decision-guide-ciam-for-apps-you-build added to the q001 facts.

findings.quote: | Directory data in AWS? | None: it [does not replicate any of your directory data](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-ad-connector-no-data-replicated) | Yes, on [two domain controllers](../facts/directory-service.md#directory-service-managed-ad-minimum-two-domain-controllers) | Yes |
findings.evidence: Two is the minimum, not a fixed count. Fact directory-service-managed-ad-minimum-two-domain-controllers: "For each AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory managed directory, AWS creates the minimum two domain controllers automatically to provide high availability. You can scale out your managed directory by creating additional domain controllers to improve your managed directory performance and availability." Same in 2-deep.md step 1 'AWS runs [two domain controllers] for you' and the A-list row '[two domain controllers] | Each AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory'. Card identity-federation-c006 already says 'a minimum of'. Fix: 'at least [two domain controllers]'.
findings.resolution: 'at least [two domain controllers]' in the 1-fast compare table, 2-deep step 1 and the A-list row ('At least [two domain controllers]').

findings.quote: To cut access now, add the user's ID to a Deny in a **service control policy** (SCP).
findings.evidence: The sentence has no fact link (fact iam-identity-center-revoke-keep-deny-12-hours supports it: "Update the Deny policy to add the user ID from step 1 in your service control policy (SCP)."), and it omits a limit that matters for Callvale: source docs/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps: "SCPs don't affect users or roles in the management account. They affect only the member accounts in your organization." Same in speak.json identity-federation-s01 follow-up 1. Fix: link the sentence and add 'in a member account'.
findings.resolution: Go deeper now reads 'To end open sessions, add the user's ID to a prepared Deny in a service control policy (SCP); SCPs [affect only member accounts](organizations-scp-no-effect-on-management-account). [If you wait 12 hours], [active sessions expire]. Remove the Deny sooner, and the user [will have restored actions with the IAM role].' speak s01 follow-up 1 adds 'in member accounts' and 'A service control policy does not reach the management account.'

findings.quote: | "the API accepts only signed-in users" | `COGNITO_USER_POOLS` authorizer | only if [the supplied token is valid](../facts/cognito.md#cognito-api-gateway-cognito-user-pools-authorizer) | requests signed with identity pool credentials: `AWS_IAM` |
findings.evidence: The linked fact's scope is 'API Gateway REST APIs' (source page 'Control access to REST APIs using Amazon Cognito user pools as an authorizer'). The signal is stated for any API. Fix: 'the REST API accepts only signed-in users'.
findings.resolution: 1-fast signal row now reads '"the REST API accepts only signed-in users"'.

findings.quote: 3. **Pick the role.** Signed-in users get the authenticated role.
findings.evidence: The authenticated role is the default; role selection can also follow rules or attributes. Fact cognito-identity-pool-enhanced-flow-one-hour-credentials: "You can configure your identity pool to select a default role, to apply attribute-based access control (ABAC) or role-based access control (RBAC) principles to role selection." Fact cognito-unauthenticated-role-more-restrictive: "You can specify default IAM roles for authenticated and unauthenticated users." Fix: 'Signed-in users get the authenticated role by default.'
findings.resolution: No word room: 2-deep.md is at its cap (2,396 of 2,400 words after the blocking fixes). 'by default' needs a link to cognito-identity-pool-role-selection-options; the step stays 'Signed-in users get the authenticated role.', which is true of the default setup the subsection teaches.

findings.quote: IAM Identity Center, with a permission set for each account.
findings.evidence: A permission set is not per account: one permission set is assigned to many accounts. Source docs/singlesignon/latest/userguide/limits: "The ProvisionPermissionSet API operation can provision a permission set using the option ALL_PROVISIONED_ACCOUNTS to, at most, 3500 AWS accounts." Fix: 'IAM Identity Center, with permission sets assigned to the accounts.'
findings.resolution: c001 back (cards add --replace) now reads 'IAM Identity Center, with permission sets assigned to the accounts.'

findings.quote: - "Launch Amazon EC2 instances in the VPC as ...": Replicated domain controllers on EC2 hold a copy of every user account, which breaks the requirement that the accounts stay in the on-premises directory.
findings.evidence: An unlinked general claim about Active Directory replication; no fact in the canon supports it. It is probably right, but the rationale could rest on a fact instead, for example the contrast with directory-service-ad-connector-no-data-replicated ('all of your directory data remains on your domain controllers'). Fix: 'Domain controllers on EC2 are part of the domain and hold its data, unlike AD Connector, with which all directory data remains on your domain controllers.'
findings.resolution: q003 option c why (wording only) now reads 'Domain controllers on EC2 join the domain and keep its data in AWS. With AD Connector, the directory data [remains on your domain controllers], as the stem requires.'

findings.evidence: The tasks gate warning T113 comes from _build/reports/cli/05.json ('missing required option --allow-unauthenticated-identities'), but the command is valid: source docs/cli/latest/reference/cognito-identity/create-identity-pool: "--allow-unauthenticated-identities | --no-allow-unauthenticated-identities (boolean) [required]", and the AWS example on the same page uses '--no-allow-unauthenticated-identities'. Do not change the command; the CLI checker does not accept the negated form of a required boolean. Record it so the fixer and finalize do not chase this warning in the chapter.
findings.resolution: Command unchanged. The CLI model helper (tools/helpers/cli_model.py) now counts --no-<name> as giving a required boolean; tasks check-cli 05: 12 commands, 0 not ok (awscli 1.46.1), so T113 passes.
